title: 14 reads lost to 3
whisper: One week, two ways to study.

creative.thesis: Two study methods race on one desk; the same marbles that make the rereaders win at five minutes drain away over a week.
creative.opening: hold: close on the open book (14 tally marks) and the closed one (3), then pull back to the two jars
creative.composition: one desk under a lamp, two lanes (REREAD left, RECALL right), each with a glass jar of 30 marbles = the 30 idea units of the text
creative.rhythm: fast setup, a hold on the 5-minute win, a day/night time-lapse for the week, a hard flip of the jars
creative.payoff: the jars drain to 12 and 18 marbles; then the viewer is asked to recall the hook number (retrieval on the viewer = the loop)
creative.sound: marble clicks for every unit, a clock tick under the week, one stamp on the flip

_note: Rendered in raea (raea/ungraded-007-recall): a study desk, two glass jars of marbles, a day/night week; cues live in the composition.

beats.say: One group read it fourteen times. The other, three. A week later, who remembered more?
In {2006|two thousand six}, two psychologists gave {180|a hundred and eighty} students a short science text.
Group one reads it for five minutes. Then again. And again. About fourteen reads.
Group two reads it once, closes it, and writes down all they remember. Three times. No corrections.
Five minutes later, the rereaders win. {83%|Eighty-three percent} to {71%|seventy-one}.
And they feel surer they'll remember it next week.
But wait a week before the test, and it flips.
Rereading feels like knowing. Recalling is what lasts.
At school, a test checks what you learned. Out here, the test is how you learn.
Careful: one lab, college students, short texts. But a big {2013|twenty thirteen} review agrees. Practice tests: high utility. Rereading: low.
So close the book. Write what you remember. Then check what you missed.
Try it now. No scrolling back. How many times did group one read it?
